questions.prompt: The Euclidean projection \(p\) of a point \(z\) onto a nonempty closed convex set \(\mathcal{C}\) is characterized by
options: \((z - p)^T (x - p) \ge 0\) for every \(x\) in \(\mathcal{C}\)
\((z - p)^T (x - p) = 0\) for every \(x\) in \(\mathcal{C}\)
\(p = z\) whenever \(z\) lies outside \(\mathcal{C}\)
\((z - p)^T (x - p) \le 0\) for every \(x\) in \(\mathcal{C}\)
questions.explanation: The vector from \(p\) to \(z\) makes an obtuse or right angle with every vector from \(p\) to another feasible point. The opposite sign is the variational inequality for a general objective, before it is specialized to the squared distance. Equality for every feasible \(x\) would force the set to be a singleton. A point outside the set is not its own projection.

questions.prompt: Project \((-1,\ 5)\) onto the box \([0,\ 2] \times [0,\ 2]\). What is the squared Euclidean distance from the point to its projection?
questions.explanation: Each coordinate is clipped to \([0,\ 2]\), so the projection is \((0,\ 2)\). The squared distance is \((-1 - 0)^2 + (5 - 2)^2 = 1 + 9 = 10\). Reporting \(1\) or \(9\) keeps only one squared gap. Reporting \(4\) clips the second coordinate to the wrong end of the interval. The projection is the nearest point of the box, and the squared length is what the Euclidean projection minimizes.

questions.prompt: If \(z\) already lies in a nonempty closed convex set, the Euclidean projection of \(z\) is
options: a different boundary point
undefined, because the distance is already zero
\(z\) itself
the origin, after a translation that moves the set
questions.explanation: The distance from \(z\) to \(z\) is zero, and no other point is closer. The obtuse-angle inequality holds because \(z - p = 0\). The origin is the projection of \(z\) only when \(z\) itself is the origin, or when the set forces that result. A zero distance is a valid projection, not a failure of the definition.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that projects a point onto a closed ball, when the point lies outside the ball. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The radial vector is the input to the length, so it comes first. The quotient uses the length, so the length comes before the division. The scaled vector uses the quotient. Adding the center last places the result on the ray from the center through the outside point, at distance equal to the radius. Scaling by the length instead of by the radius over the length lands past the sphere.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 220" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a disk at the origin</title><line x1="28" y1="112" x2="252" y2="112"/><polygon points="252,112 245.6,114.7 245.6,109.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="140" y1="196" x2="140" y2="28"/><polygon points="140,28 142.7,34.4 137.3,34.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="246" y="128" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="148" y="32" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><circle cx="140" cy="112" r="64" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.12"/><circle cx="140" cy="112" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A filled disk centered at the origin.
steps: Subtract the center from the outside point to get the radial vector.
Compute the Euclidean length of that radial vector.
Divide the radius by that length.
Scale the radial vector by that quotient and add the center.

questions.prompt: Let \(p = (1,\ 0)\) be the projection of \(z = (2,\ 0)\) onto the closed unit disk. Which of these points \(x\) satisfy \((z - p)^T (x - p) \le 0\)?
questions.explanation:
Here \(z - p = (1,\ 0)\), so the product is the first coordinate of \(x - p\).
• \((0,\ 0)\) gives \(-1\).
• \((0,\ 1)\) gives \(-1\).
• \((1,\ 0)\) gives \(0\).
• \((3/5,\ 4/5)\) gives \(3/5 - 1 = -2/5\).
• \((2,\ 0)\) gives \(1\), which is positive.
The inequality is required at every point of the disk, including the projection itself. The outside point \(z\) is not one of those points.

questions.prompt: The point \((a,\ b)\) lies outside the disk of radius \(r\) centered at the origin. The first coordinate of its Euclidean projection onto that disk equals
questions.explanation: The projection is the radius times the unit vector from the origin toward \((a,\ b)\). The first coordinate is \(r a / \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\). Every name appears. Dropping \(r\) returns a unit-vector coordinate. Dividing by the squared length, instead of the length, is a different scaling. Using \(a + b\) in the numerator mixes the two coordinates.

questions.prompt: A note projects \((4,\ 1)\) onto the box \([0,\ 2] \times [0,\ 2]\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The set is the stated box. The first coordinate \(4\) is above \(2\), and \(1\) lies between \(0\) and \(2\). Clipping sends the first coordinate to \(2\) and leaves the second at \(1\), so the projection is \((2,\ 1)\). The point \((4,\ 1)\) is outside the box, so it cannot be the projection. Leaving an infeasible point unchanged is the rule only when the point is already feasible.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 260 200" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a shaded quadrant</title><line x1="48" y1="168" x2="236" y2="168"/><polygon points="236,168 229.6,170.7 229.6,165.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="48" y1="180" x2="48" y2="24"/><polygon points="48,24 50.7,30.4 45.3,30.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="230" y="184" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="56" y="20" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><rect x="48" y="48" width="150" height="120" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/></svg>
steps: The feasible set is the box \([0,\ 2] \times [0,\ 2]\).
The first coordinate of \((4,\ 1)\) lies above \(2\), and the second lies in \([0,\ 2]\).
Clipping replaces an out-of-range coordinate by the nearest endpoint and keeps an in-range coordinate.
reasons: The projection is \((2,\ 1)\). The point \((4,\ 1)\) lies outside the box.
The second coordinate \(1\) does not lie in \([0,\ 2]\).
Clipping is not the Euclidean projection onto an axis-aligned box.

questions.prompt: Project \((6,\ 8)\) onto the disk of radius \(5\) centered at the origin. What is the first coordinate of the projection?
questions.explanation: The point has length \(\sqrt{36 + 64} = 10\), which is outside the disk. The projection is \((5/10)(6,\ 8) = (3,\ 4)\). The first coordinate is \(3\). Reporting \(4\) is the second coordinate. Reporting \(6\) leaves the point unscaled. Reporting \(10\) is the length of the original point. The result lies on the ray from the origin and on the circle.

questions.prompt: The nearest-point projection of every \(z\) is a single point of the set when the set is
options: a closed disk with two declared projections of the same outside point
nonempty, closed, and convex
any nonempty set, including a pair of isolated points
an open disk that does not contain \(z\)
questions.explanation: Closedness gives existence and convexity gives uniqueness for the Euclidean nearest point. Two isolated points are not convex, and the midpoint of the segment between them is equally close to both. An open disk need not contain its nearest boundary point, so the projection in the set can fail to exist. A closed disk has one projection of each outside point.

questions.prompt: In the norm \(\lVert v\rVert_H = \sqrt{v^T H v}\) with \(H\) symmetric positive definite, the projection \(p\) of \(z\) satisfies
options: \((z - p)^T H (x - p) \le 0\) for every feasible \(x\)
the Euclidean obtuse-angle test, for every such \(H\)
the same point as the Euclidean projection, for every convex set
questions.explanation: The angle test is taken in the inner product \(u^T H v\). The Euclidean test is the special case \(H = I\). A positive definite \(H\) that stretches one axis moves the nearest point on a slanted set. Nothing in the inequality says \(H p = z\) unless the set is a singleton at that location.

questions.prompt: Using \(H = \mathrm{diag}(4,\ 1)\), project \(z = (3,\ 4)\) onto the half-space \(x_1 + x_2 \le 2\). What is the first coordinate of the projection?
questions.explanation: \(H^{-1} = \mathrm{diag}(1/4,\ 1)\) and \(a = (1,\ 1)\). The excess \(a^T z - 2\) equals \(5\). The denominator \(a^T H^{-1} a\) equals \(5/4\), so the multiplier is \(4\). The correction is \(4 H^{-1} a = (1,\ 4)\). The projection is \((3,\ 4) - (1,\ 4) = (2,\ 0)\). The first coordinate is \(2\). The Euclidean projection onto the same half-space is a different point, because it uses \(H = I\). Reporting \(3\) leaves the infeasible point unchanged.

questions.prompt: The Euclidean projection of a point onto an axis-aligned box
options: adds one common constant to every coordinate
needs a matrix factorization even when the point is already inside
can land outside the box
clips each coordinate to its own interval
questions.explanation: The squared Euclidean distance separates across coordinates, and so does the box. Each coordinate is the nearest point of its interval, which is clipping. A common additive shift would preserve differences between coordinates and can leave the box. An interior point is already feasible, so its projection is itself and no factorization is required. The clipped point lies in the box by construction.
